I’ve been thinking about the spaces between things — not the things themselves, but what happens in the gaps. A piano piece isn’t just the notes; it’s the silence after a chord, the held breath before the next phrase. If you removed the rests, the music would turn into a blur, an unbroken noise that means nothing. Sometimes meaning lives mostly in the absence.

You can feel this everywhere if you look. The pause between two people talking, when something unsaid hangs in the air and changes the temperature of the room. The white margins around words on a page, which give the text room to breathe. The split second after you wake up, before memory arrives and tells you who you are, what day it is, what you’re supposed to worry about. That moment is very short and very clean, like touching water before the ripples start.

We’re not good at emptiness, though. We fill it. We reach for our phones when we’re in line, when we’re stopped at a red light, when the conversation lags. We’re uncomfortable with the unoccupied minute. But maybe the quality of our attention is shaped more by what we refuse to fill than by what we pour into every opening. Maybe a person who can tolerate a quiet room is a person who can actually hear.

I remember learning that fallow fields are left empty on purpose. The soil rests, regains nutrients, and produces better crops later. We have this idea that fallow is lazy, a lack of doing, a waste of time. But there are kinds of rest that are not absence of work — they are the deep, underground work, the slow repair, the accumulation of what will later surface as growth. I think the same is true of the mind. The thoughts that matter sometimes grow in the fallow hours, the ones we don’t schedule or fill.

Even memory works by cutting things out. We forget most of our days; we forget the faces of people we used to know; we forget how a particular room smelled, how the light fell on a certain afternoon. And yet this forgetting is not a failure. It is a kind of editing. We keep the scenes that matter, the faces that still move us, the moments that quietly shaped what we became. The rest recedes into a haze, and the haze is peaceful. We can’t keep everything. To remember everything would be to drown in the detail of being alive, unable to move forward because the past weighs too much.

I’ve also noticed that the best writing leaves gaps. It doesn’t say everything; it suggests. The reader’s imagination fills the blank space, and in that act of filling, the story becomes theirs. A sentence that ends just before something is said can be more intimate than one that spells it out. The unsaid is a kind of doorway — through it, the reader walks into the text and becomes a co-creator. I love those moments in books where I catch myself imagining what the character is feeling, and I realize the author never described it, and yet it’s there, in me, put there by an absence.

Maybe that’s what we’re doing when we sit with someone without needing to talk. We’re being together in the gaps. The silence isn’t empty; it’s full of trust. It says: I don’t need to perform, and you don’t either. We can just be here. That might be one of the deepest kinds of intimacy there is — the willingness to leave the spaces unoccupied, to let the quiet speak.

So I’m trying to let more gaps exist in my days. Not waiting for something, not filling, just letting the row be empty. It’s hard. It feels like doing nothing. But maybe doing nothing is sometimes a way of being ready for whatever comes next, or of simply being here at all. Some things only arrive in silence. If you keep chattering, you won’t hear them knock.
